Tutorial 3: Finding and validating hits

Emanuel Michele Soda

Istituto Europeo Oncologia (IEO), Milano, Italy
emanuelsoda@gmail.com

Elena Ceccacci

Istituto Europeo Oncologia (IEO), Milano, Italy
elena.ceccacci@ieo.it

2026-10-16

Source: vignettes/Tutorial_3_Finding_hits.Rmd
Tutorial_3_Finding_hits.Rmd

About this tutorial

A hit is a gene whose barcodes change consistently in the treated samples compared with the control samples. In a dropout (loss of function) screen the interesting hits are usually depleted: their knockdown kills the cells only in the presence of the treatment.

This tutorial explains, step by step:

  1. how to tell ScreenR which samples to compare;
  2. the statistical methods to find hits and how to read their results;
  3. how to combine the methods;
  4. how to check the candidate hits before trusting them.

It continues from the object of the previous tutorials:

library(ScreenR)
#> Warning: replacing previous import 'S4Arrays::makeNindexFromArrayViewport' by
#> 'DelayedArray::makeNindexFromArrayViewport' when loading 'SummarizedExperiment'
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)

counts <- count_table
colnames(counts) <- c(
    "Barcode", "Time1", "Time2", "Time3_TRT_A", "Time3_TRT_B", "Time3_TRT_C",
    "Time3_CTRL_A", "Time3_CTRL_B", "Time3_CTRL_C",
    "Time4_TRT_A", "Time4_TRT_B", "Time4_TRT_C",
    "Time4_CTRL_A", "Time4_CTRL_B", "Time4_CTRL_C"
)
counts <- filter(counts, Barcode != "*")
groups <- factor(c(
    "T1/T2", "T1/T2",
    rep("Time3_TRT", 3), rep("Time3_CTRL", 3),
    rep("Time4_TRT", 3), rep("Time4_CTRL", 3)
))

object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
object <- normalize_data(object)
object <- compute_data_table(object)

Overview of the methods

Method Function Unit Gives an FDR Uses replicates
Gene-level Z-score test find_gene_zscore_hit() Compares the mean Z-score of the barcodes of each gene with random sets of barcodes Yes With compute_barcode_statistics()
CAMERA find_camera_hit() Tests whether the barcodes of a gene change more than the others Yes Yes
ROAST find_roast_hit() Tests whether the barcodes of a gene change Yes Yes
Time course find_time_hit() Tests whether the treatment effect changes over time Yes Yes
Legacy Z-score rules find_zscore_hit(), find_robust_zscore_hit() Counts barcodes below the median Z-score No No

The FDR (false discovery rate) is the expected proportion of false hits among the genes you call hits: with an FDR cut off of 5%, about 1 in 20 of the reported genes is expected to be a false positive. Each method returns only the genes with FDR <= fdr (default 0.05); use fdr = 1 to get all the genes and rank them yourself.

Step 1: which samples to compare

CAMERA, ROAST and the replicate-aware statistics use a linear model, which needs two things:

  • a design matrix, which says which group each sample belongs to;
  • a contrast, which says which groups to compare.

create_design_matrix() builds the design matrix from the groups of the object: one column per group, and a 1 in the column of the group of each sample. Group names that are not valid R names are changed (T1/T2 becomes T1.T2).

design <- create_design_matrix(object)
design
#>    T1.T2 Time3_CTRL Time3_TRT Time4_CTRL Time4_TRT
#> 1      1          0         0          0         0
#> 2      1          0         0          0         0
#> 3      0          0         1          0         0
#> 4      0          0         1          0         0
#> 5      0          0         1          0         0
#> 6      0          1         0          0         0
#> 7      0          1         0          0         0
#> 8      0          1         0          0         0
#> 9      0          0         0          0         1
#> 10     0          0         0          0         1
#> 11     0          0         0          0         1
#> 12     0          0         0          1         0
#> 13     0          0         0          1         0
#> 14     0          0         0          1         0
#> attr(,"assign")
#> [1] 1 1 1 1 1
#> attr(,"contrasts")
#> attr(,"contrasts")$groups
#> [1] "contr.treatment"

create_contrast() builds the comparison between groups by name: here treated against control at each time point.

contrast_time3 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time3_TRT", control = "Time3_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time4_TRT", control = "Time4_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4
#>      T1.T2 Time3_CTRL  Time3_TRT Time4_CTRL  Time4_TRT 
#>          0          0          0         -1          1

The contrast gives +1 to the treated group and -1 to the control group: the result is the treated minus the control. With several groups on one side (for example treatment = c("Time3_TRT", "Time4_TRT")) their average is used.

Common mistake. Do not build the design with model.matrix(~ groups) and rename its columns: the first group becomes the intercept and the columns are in alphabetical order, so the names end up on the wrong columns and the wrong samples are compared. create_design_matrix() and create_contrast() avoid this.

The examples below compare treated and control samples at Time4.

Step 2: the Z-score method

Fold changes and Z-scores

compute_metrics() averages the replicates of the treated and of the control samples of one time point and computes for each barcode:

Column Meaning
Treated, Control Mean normalized count
Log2FC log2((Treated + 0.5) / (Control + 0.5)): negative means depleted in the treated samples
Zscore Log2FC standardized with the mean and standard deviation of all barcodes
ZscoreRobust Log2FC standardized with the median and MAD, less sensitive to outliers

The treatment and control arguments are values of the Treatment column of get_sample_table(), and day a value of its Day column.

metrics_time4 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time4"
)
head(metrics_time4)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   Barcode Gene     Treated Control Log2FC Zscore ZscoreRobust Day   Treatment
#>   <fct>   <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>        <dbl> <chr> <chr>    
#> 1 1       Gene_386   245.    279.  -0.187 -0.303       -0.482 Time4 TRT      
#> 2 10      Gene_519    74.3   118.  -0.665 -1.30        -1.85  Time4 TRT      
#> 3 100     Gene_84     38.6    32.1  0.262  0.634        0.806 Time4 TRT      
#> 4 1000    Gene_350   126.    115.   0.138  0.376        0.452 Time4 TRT      
#> 5 10001   Gene_379   412.    453.  -0.138 -0.200       -0.340 Time4 TRT      
#> 6 10002   Gene_379   191.    207.  -0.116 -0.155       -0.278 Time4 TRT

plot_zscore_distribution() compares the Z-scores of several time points: a treatment with an effect gives a longer left tail at the later time point.

metrics_time3 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time3"
)
plot_zscore_distribution(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    alpha = 0.6
)

Gene-level test

find_gene_zscore_hit() computes for each gene the mean Z-score of its barcodes and asks how often a random set of barcodes of the same size has a score at least as low (direction = "Down"). The random sets are drawn many times (n_permutations), so the p-value needs no assumption on the distribution of the Z-scores; seed makes it reproducible. The p-values are then corrected for testing many genes (FDR).

If the library has control genes, their gene name can be given with control_genes (for example control_genes = "non-targeting"): the random sets are then drawn from the controls, which cannot contain true hits. Do this only if the controls behave like genes without effect. Non-targeting shRNAs often do not: targeting shRNAs are usually somewhat depleted compared with them, so every gene looks depleted (in the K562 screen of ScreenR this called hundreds of non-essential genes). Check first that the controls have the same scores as genes known to have no effect; when in doubt, keep the default. statistic = "median" uses the median instead of the mean, which is less affected by a single barcode with a strong (possibly off-target) effect.

With reference = "empirical" the gene scores are compared with an empirical null instead: the distribution of the scores of the genes without effect, estimated from the centre of the distribution of all the genes (plot_empirical_null() shows it). The hits do not make it conservative, and it accounts for the barcodes of a gene varying together, which makes the random sets of barcodes give too small p-values, especially in shRNA screens (see ?find_gene_zscore_hit and Tutorial 4). It needs a library with hundreds of genes, most of them without effect.

gene_zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(metrics_time4, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NBarcodes  Score Log2FC    PValue    FDR
#>   <chr>        <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_364        12 -1.55  -0.473 0.0000500 0.0267
#> 2 Gene_296        10 -1.31  -0.499 0.000460  0.123 
#> 3 Gene_322        10 -1.13  -0.386 0.00148   0.263 
#> 4 Gene_419        10 -1.08  -0.311 0.00209   0.279 
#> 5 Gene_352        10 -1.02  -0.455 0.00318   0.340 
#> 6 Gene_422        10 -0.951 -0.430 0.00455   0.405
Column Meaning
NBarcodes Number of barcodes of the gene
Score Mean Z-score of the barcodes
Log2FC Median log2 fold change of the barcodes
PValue, FDR Significance

Using the replicates

compute_metrics() averages the replicates, so it cannot tell a consistent barcode from a noisy one. compute_barcode_statistics() tests each barcode with edgeR, using the variability between replicates, and returns a Z-score that can be used by find_gene_zscore_hit() in the same way. This is the recommended input.

barcode_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(
    object, design, contrast_time4
)
head(barcode_statistics)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   Barcode Gene     Log2FC logCPM     F PValue   FDR Zscore
#>   <chr>   <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 10208   Gene_380  0.109   8.56 0.438 0.510  0.835  0.658
#> 2 10502   Gene_380 -0.480   4.97 0.748 0.390  0.765 -0.859
#> 3 10796   Gene_380 -0.665   6.61 2.49  0.120  0.515 -1.56 
#> 4 11089   Gene_380 -0.169   8.44 0.992 0.323  0.716 -0.988
#> 5 11382   Gene_380 -0.651   5.62 1.44  0.235  0.643 -1.19 
#> 6 11675   Gene_380 -0.286   9.66 6.71  0.0119 0.219 -2.51

gene_zscore_edger <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics, fdr = 1,
    seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore_edger)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NBarcodes Score Log2FC   PValue   FDR
#>   <chr>        <int> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173        10 -1.58 -0.521 0.000240 0.128
#> 2 Gene_422        10 -1.45 -0.451 0.000700 0.187
#> 3 Gene_15         10 -1.37 -0.321 0.00131  0.233
#> 4 Gene_296        10 -1.31 -0.493 0.00187  0.250
#> 5 Gene_370        10 -1.24 -0.394 0.00304  0.280
#> 6 Gene_168        10 -1.21 -0.256 0.00355  0.280

Legacy rules

find_zscore_hit() and find_robust_zscore_hit() call a gene a hit when more than number_barcode of its barcodes are below the median Z-score. They are kept for compatibility, but they do not give a p-value and many genes without an effect pass them by chance (about 17% with 10 barcodes and number_barcode = 6): prefer find_gene_zscore_hit().

nrow(find_zscore_hit(metrics_time4, number_barcode = 6))
#> [1] 97

Step 3: CAMERA and ROAST

Both test the barcodes of each gene as a set, using edgeR on the raw counts.

  • CAMERA asks whether the barcodes of a gene change more than the other barcodes (a competitive test), taking into account the correlation between barcodes.
  • ROAST asks whether the barcodes of a gene change at all (a self-contained test). It uses random rotations: set seed to get the same result every time, and use many rotations (nrot, default 9999) for a real analysis; here 999 keep the tutorial fast. With method = "fry" the same test is computed exactly, without rotations: it is faster and its p-values are not limited by the number of rotations.

CAMERA becomes conservative when many genes have an effect, because the other barcodes it compares with then include true hits; ROAST and fry do not have this limitation. On the other hand ROAST and fry test each gene on its own barcodes, so they rely on the variability between replicates: they need replicates in both groups, have little power with two replicates or noisy data, and find almost nothing when the control is a single sample (for example a plasmid library). The p-values of all three are one-sided, for the requested direction.

number_barcode sets the minimum number of barcodes (more than number_barcode) a gene needs to be tested, and direction chooses depleted ("Down") or enriched ("Up") genes.

camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast_time4, fdr = 1)
head(camera)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NGenes Direction   PValue    FDR Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <fct>        <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173     10 Down      0.000214 0.0882 -0.515
#> 2 Gene_422     10 Down      0.000418 0.0882 -0.433
#> 3 Gene_296     10 Down      0.000495 0.0882 -0.508
#> 4 Gene_352     10 Down      0.00200  0.232  -0.467
#> 5 Gene_87      10 Down      0.00250  0.232  -0.436
#> 6 Gene_370     10 Down      0.00295  0.232  -0.344

roast <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast_time4,
    nrot = 999, seed = 42, fdr = 1
)
head(select(roast, Gene, NGenes, PropDown, PropUp, Direction, PValue, FDR,
    Log2FC))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 8
#>   Gene     NGenes PropDown PropUp Direction PValue    FDR Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <int>    <dbl>  <dbl> <fct>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_296     10      0.6    0   Down      0.0005 0.0534 -0.508
#> 2 Gene_173     10      0.5    0.1 Down      0.0005 0.0534 -0.515
#> 3 Gene_412     10      0.5    0.1 Down      0.0005 0.0534 -0.325
#> 4 Gene_422     10      0.5    0   Down      0.0005 0.0534 -0.433
#> 5 Gene_325     10      0.3    0.1 Down      0.0005 0.0534 -0.246
#> 6 Gene_15      10      0.5    0   Down      0.001  0.0668 -0.325
Column Meaning
NGenes Number of barcodes of the gene
Direction Down or Up
PValue, FDR Significance
PropDown, PropUp (ROAST) Proportion of barcodes going down or up
Log2FC Median log2 fold change of the barcodes

How many genes pass different FDR cut offs:

fdr_levels <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25)
tibble(
    FDR = fdr_levels,
    zscore = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(gene_zscore_edger$FDR <= x),
        1L),
    CAMERA = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(camera$FDR <= x), 1L),
    ROAST = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(roast$FDR <= x), 1L)
)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>     FDR zscore CAMERA ROAST
#>   <dbl>  <int>  <int> <int>
#> 1  0.05      0      0     0
#> 2  0.1       0      3    11
#> 3  0.25      4      7    55

The effect of the treatment in this example is weak: no gene reaches an FDR of 5%. In the rest of the tutorial we use 25% to illustrate the steps; in your own analysis, choose the cut off before looking at the results and report it.

alpha <- 0.25

Step 4: the time course

When the screen has several time points, find_time_hit() asks whether the treatment effect changes over time, with one model for all the time points instead of one analysis per time point. Untreated and treated samples each follow a line over time; the method tests the difference between the slopes. Early samples taken before the treatment can be added as baseline. The time points are given in order with days and are treated as equally spaced.

time_hit <- find_time_hit(object,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    baseline = c("Time1", "Time2"),
    days = c("Time1", "Time2", "Time3", "Time4"),
    fdr = 1
)
head(time_hit)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   Gene     NGenes Direction      PValue       FDR Log2FC
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <fct>           <dbl>     <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_372     12 Down      0.000000157 0.0000836 -0.974
#> 2 Gene_296     10 Down      0.000000706 0.000135  -1.17 
#> 3 Gene_364     12 Down      0.000000760 0.000135  -1.01 
#> 4 Gene_412     10 Down      0.000112    0.0149    -0.815
#> 5 Gene_370     10 Down      0.000565    0.0604    -0.389
#> 6 Gene_349     10 Down      0.00376     0.318     -0.192

Here Log2FC is the change of the treatment log2 fold change per time point: a negative value means that the depletion grows over time. In this dataset 4 genes have an FDR below 5% (Gene_372, Gene_296, Gene_364, Gene_412): the time course model is more powerful here than the comparison at a single time point, because it uses all the samples.

Step 5: combining the methods

The methods look at the data in different ways, so genes found by several of them are the most convincing. plot_common_hit() shows the overlap between the hits of three methods:

plot_common_hit(
    hit_zscore = filter(gene_zscore_edger, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_camera = filter(camera, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_roast = filter(roast, FDR <= alpha),
    show_elements = FALSE, show_percentage = FALSE
)

find_common_hit() returns the genes found by at least common_in methods:

common <- find_common_hit(
    filter(gene_zscore_edger, FDR <= alpha),
    filter(camera, FDR <= alpha),
    filter(roast, FDR <= alpha),
    common_in = 2
)
common
#> [1] "Gene_173" "Gene_422" "Gene_15"  "Gene_296" "Gene_352" "Gene_87"  "Gene_370"

summarise_hits() puts the FDR of every method in one table. NMethods counts the methods in which the gene passes the cut off, and MaxFDR (the largest FDR) is a conservative score to rank the genes supported by all the methods. Pass the tables computed with fdr = 1, so that every gene has a value.

summary <- summarise_hits(
    list(
        zscore = gene_zscore_edger, camera = camera,
        roast = roast, time = time_hit
    ),
    fdr = alpha
)
head(summary, 10)
#> # A tibble: 10 × 8
#>    Gene     FDR_zscore FDR_camera FDR_roast FDR_time NMethods MaxFDR Hit  
#>    <chr>         <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <lgl>
#>  1 Gene_296      0.250     0.0882    0.0534 0.000135        4  0.250 TRUE 
#>  2 Gene_370      0.280     0.232     0.111  0.0604          3  0.280 FALSE
#>  3 Gene_349      0.390     0.263     0.0668 0.318           1  0.390 FALSE
#>  4 Gene_352      0.280     0.232     0.157  0.508           2  0.508 FALSE
#>  5 Gene_87       0.280     0.232     0.207  0.508           2  0.508 FALSE
#>  6 Gene_422      0.187     0.0882    0.0534 0.545           3  0.545 FALSE
#>  7 Gene_412      0.590     0.306     0.0534 0.0149          2  0.590 FALSE
#>  8 Gene_325      0.649     0.738     0.0534 0.318           1  0.738 FALSE
#>  9 Gene_173      0.128     0.0882    0.0534 0.742           3  0.742 FALSE
#> 10 Gene_168      0.280     0.380     0.153  0.742           1  0.742 FALSE

The column Hit is TRUE when the gene passes the cut off in every method (MaxFDR <= alpha). A note on interpretation: the combined list does not have a guaranteed false discovery rate, so treat it as a short list of candidates to validate. In this dataset 1 gene(s) pass all four methods at 25%, so below we check the genes found by at least two of the three methods of the Venn diagram.

Step 6: checking the candidates

Statistics can produce false positives, so look at the data of each candidate.

candidates <- head(common, 2)
candidates
#> [1] "Gene_173" "Gene_422"

Trend over time

plot_trend() shows the mean frequency of the barcodes of a gene in the chosen samples (group_var takes values of the Treatment column). A depleted hit goes down in the treated samples but not in the controls.

plot_trend(object,
    genes = candidates, group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "TRT"),
    nrow = 1, ncol = 2
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    ggtitle("Treated samples")


plot_trend(object,
    genes = candidates, group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "CTRL"),
    nrow = 1, ncol = 2
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    ggtitle("Control samples")

Distribution of the barcodes

plot_boxplot() shows the frequencies of all the barcodes of a gene in each sample:

plot_boxplot(object,
    genes = candidates[1], group_var = c("TRT", "CTRL"),
    fill_var = "Treatment"
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Barcode by barcode

A real hit should be supported by most of its barcodes, not by one or two. plot_barcode_trend() shows the log2 fold change of each barcode over the time points:

plot_barcode_trend(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    genes = candidates[1]
)
#> $Gene_173

plot_barcode_hit() ranks all the barcodes by their log2 fold change and places the barcodes of a gene on the ranking (vertical lines): most lines on the left side means that the gene is depleted. The line on top shows where the barcodes of the gene are concentrated (above 1, dashed line), and the bottom panel shows their log2 fold changes (show_log2fc = FALSE hides it):

plot_barcode_hit(object, design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, gene = candidates[1]
)

find_discordant_barcodes() lists the barcodes that behave very differently from the other barcodes of their gene, which may have off-target effects:

discordant <- find_discordant_barcodes(metrics_time4, threshold = 3)
filter(discordant, Gene %in% candidates)
#> # A tibble: 0 × 5
#> # ℹ 5 variables: Barcode <fct>, Gene <chr>, Log2FC <dbl>, GeneLog2FC <dbl>,
#> #   Deviation <dbl>

Additional filters

Two filters can remove candidates that are not convincing:

  • filter_by_slope() keeps the genes whose frequency decreases more over time in the treated samples than in the control samples;
  • filter_by_variance() removes the genes whose barcodes disagree too much (variance of the barcode log2 fold changes above variance).
filter_by_slope(object,
    genes = candidates,
    group_var_treatment = c("Time1", "Time2", "TRT"),
    group_var_control = c("Time1", "Time2", "CTRL")
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   Gene     slope_control slope_treatment
#>   <chr>            <dbl>           <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173          7.07          -11.4 
#> 2 Gene_422          5.38           -5.96

filter_by_variance(object,
    genes = candidates, matrix_model = design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, variance = 0.5
) %>%
    distinct(Gene, Variance)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   Gene     Variance
#>   <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 Gene_173    0.324
#> 2 Gene_422    0.227

Summary

Step What to do
1 create_design_matrix() and create_contrast() for the comparison
2 compute_barcode_statistics() + find_gene_zscore_hit()
3 find_camera_hit() and find_roast_hit() (with seed)
4 find_time_hit() if there are several time points
5 plot_common_hit() and summarise_hits()
6 plot_trend(), plot_boxplot(), plot_barcode_trend(), plot_barcode_hit(), find_discordant_barcodes()

Choose the FDR cut off before the analysis, report it, and validate the candidates experimentally.
